title: What segregation cost jazz between 1926 and 1936
summary: Jones says musicians were kept from playing with whom they wished, and the music lost much because of social conditions.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: that we recapitulated. He didn't realize, as I said, it wasn't fashionable. But it's very difficult, Milt, can you imagine if we were all allowed the privilege with the social conditions being what they were - if we were all allowed the privilege 45 musicians to play with who we want to play with and be left alone, from 1926 to 1936 we lost a whole lot of good music. We lost a whole lot of good peoples at the time, they couldn't get on recording dates, they couldn't get on no jobs, they had to play over here. Now just imagine if we'd have just been left alone, not like doctors, lawyers, and what have you - just leave us alone and let us play with who we want to play with, play in any club we want to play with, because unless we play around certain peoples we don't get it, you know. It's an economic thing; it's a social thing and we must protect ourselves, you understand that. Complexity Self-preservation, you see. But through the maze of the peoples of the world stood this.
